title: the women went to the tomb first
hook: the women went to the tomb first

segments.voice: Yesterday: the cross, Rome's execution on a Friday. Your line was the worst thing is not the last thing. Now, the Sunday.
screen: `THE WORST THING IS NOT THE LAST THING.` → `DAY 19.`

segments.voice: It's very early on a Sunday, first light. Three women are walking to a grave, carrying spices. Their friend was executed on Friday, and there wasn't time to prepare his body before the Sabbath, so they're going now. It's the last thing you can do for someone you love. And on the way, they realize they have a problem. The tomb is sealed with a big stone, and none of them can move it. Mark's Gospel keeps the question they ask each other on the road: "Who shall roll us away the stone from the door of the sepulchre?"
screen: `SUNDAY. FIRST LIGHT.` → `THREE WOMEN, CARRYING SPICES.` → `WHO WILL MOVE THE STONE?`

segments.voice: Easter. In most of the world its name comes from Pascha, from the Hebrew word for Passover, because it happened in Passover week. Where the English word Easter comes from, nobody is completely sure. In Mark, the women arrive, and the stone is already rolled back. Inside sits a young man dressed in white, who tells them: "he is risen; he is not here: behold the place where they laid him." And the oldest copies of Mark end almost right there. The women run from the tomb, trembling, and say nothing to anyone, "for they were afraid." Fear, and an empty room. Most scholars agree the longer endings in many Bibles were added later, and many churches still read them. Another Gospel tells it closer up. Mary Magdalene comes alone, while it's still dark, and finds the stone gone. She stays outside, crying. A man asks why she's weeping, and she thinks he's the gardener. Then he says one word. Her name. "Mary." And she knows him. Now notice who's there first. Not Peter. Not the twelve. Women, in a world where a woman's word counted for little. Every Gospel puts them at the tomb first. Easter is the center of the Christian year. Christians say Jesus rose from the dead, and that death doesn't get the last word. On Easter morning many greet each other: Christ is risen. And the answer comes back: he is risen indeed.
screen: `PASCHA — FROM PASSOVER.` · `"HE IS RISEN; HE IS NOT HERE."` · `MARY. SHE KNOWS HIM.` · `THE WOMEN WERE THERE FIRST.` · then, large: `THE STONE IS ALREADY MOVED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and breathe. Think of a stone in your life right now: something heavy in the way, that you've been worrying about on the road before you've even gotten there. Name it. Now, just for this minute, picture walking up and finding it already moved. Don't plan how. Don't argue with it. Just let yourself feel the relief, and breathe into it. If you pray, you can hand the stone over. If you don't, notice how much of the weight was the worrying.
Easter. Pascha. The morning the stone was moved and the tomb was empty. Nineteenth word.
Your line: the stone is already moved. The women worried about it the whole way there. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Christians celebrate Easter as their greatest feast, often with a vigil the night before or a service at sunrise. Many greet each other with "Christ is risen" and answer "he is risen indeed." Orthodox churches often keep Easter on a later date, by an older calendar.

notes: The ending of Mark (oldest manuscripts end at 16:8; 16:9–20 later) is stated as the majority scholarly view; many churches treat the longer ending as scripture. Confirm the phrasing is fair to both.
'A woman's word counted for little' in first-century courts is commonly argued; confirm the wording.
Origin of the English word 'Easter' left open on purpose (Bede's Eostre is debated).
Mark names three women (Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, Salome); John has Mary Magdalene alone. Both accounts are kept as each Gospel tells it.
